messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mai has owned the small specialty grocery store on the corner for twenty years, its shelves stocked with familiar spices and imported teas. Now, at fifty-seven, she finds the familiar space has become a landscape of potential threats. The crisis began eight months ago, when her son, visiting for dinner, collapsed in her kitchen. The terrifying hours that followed are a blur of disconnected images: the shocking crimson on the white linoleum, the paramedics with their urgent movements, the tangle of tubes and IV drips that soon surrounded him in the intensive care unit. For two days, doctors struggled to diagnose the internal hemorrhage, a period of agonizing uncertainty where Mai felt a profound sense of helplessness, a conviction that the very people meant to save him were failing. This belief, that she should have done more to protect him and that the institution she trusted had let her down, settled deep within her.

In the months since her son’s recovery, Mai has found herself living in a state of constant, exhausting vigilance. She is unable to relax, even at home with her husband, and spends her days scanning her surroundings for any sign of danger. Feeling this afraid all the time, she has eventually come to accept the conclusion her body keeps offering: that she is fundamentally unable to keep her family safe and that the world is a hostile place. This pervasive sense of threat makes her hyper-aware of any reminder of the hospital; the sight of a medical drama on television can make her heart pound, and she now insists on doing the inventory at her shop herself to avoid seeing the red ink on supplier invoices, which feels too much like blood. This feeling of being perpetually unsafe often triggers fragmented sensory replays of the trauma. It’s rarely a clear picture; more often, it is a sudden, gut-wrenching wave of the same terror and powerlessness she felt in the ICU waiting room, an emotion without an image attached. This raw feeling only serves to reinforce her appraisal of the world as a hostile place where she is fundamentally unable to keep her family safe.

The memory of the event itself remains stubbornly inaccessible when she tries to grasp it. When her husband encourages her to talk about it, Mai finds she knows what happened but is unable to find the words to form a coherent story. It exists instead as a collection of potent, disjointed fragments. This fragmentation fuels her negative beliefs about herself and the world. The visceral memory of her own helplessness solidifies into the conviction that she failed to protect her son, while the memory of the doctors’ initial confusion hardens into a deep sense of injustice. This belief that she is inadequate and the world is untrustworthy means she moves through ordinary days as if they were mined—every ambiguity becomes a potential signal of threat. In turn, these shards of memory make her exquisitely sensitive to triggers in her daily life. A customer with a simple bandage on their finger can bring the entire edifice of her fear crashing down. The sight doesn't call forth a narrative; rather, the trigger launches the raw, wordless emotion of the memory, which immediately validates her appraisal that the situation was deeply unfair and that she was powerless.

These powerful convictions—that she failed, that the system failed, that the world is unjust—have become the engine of her daily life, compelling her toward a set of rigid, self-defeating strategies. To manage the unbearable guilt, she actively tries to erase the memory, pushing away any thought of the hospital the moment it arises. She seeks constant reassurance, calling her son multiple times a day under the guise of casual conversation, needing to hear his voice to believe he is okay. She has also begun to avoid anything that might provoke a strong feeling, positive or negative, turning down invitations from friends and keeping her interactions with customers brief and superficial. But these attempts to control her inner world have backfired. The effort to suppress the memory only seems to make it erupt more forcefully at unexpected moments, which in turn keeps her perpetually on edge, unable to relax. Her avoidance of potential triggers has paradoxically made her scan for them more intensely, making her world feel smaller and more dangerous. Each time she asks for reassurance, it subtly reinforces the deep-seated belief that she cannot trust her own perceptions and is not equipped to handle a crisis.

The cycle came to a head last week. Mai had a routine check-up with her doctor, an appointment she had postponed twice. Sitting in the examination room, the sight of the sterile equipment and the needle on the tray was an overwhelming trigger. A wave of pure panic washed over her, a physical reaction so strong she felt she couldn't breathe. It was the hospital all over again—the same wordless terror, the same conviction of impending doom. She fled the office before the doctor even entered, the memory fragment confirming her belief that she was broken and had failed even at the simple task of caring for her own health. She spent the rest of the day trying to block out the experience while simultaneously calling her son’s phone, desperate for the comfort of his voice. It was this incident, her complete inability to endure basic medical care, that finally convinced her husband they needed to seek help. Mai agreed, arriving at her first therapy session unable to articulate what she wanted, only that she could no longer live inside this tightening loop of fear.
